title: We Wish to Inform You That Tomorrow We Will Be Killed with Our Families: Stories from Rwanda
author: Philip Gourevitch
target_audience: Readers interested in African history and politics
Students and scholars of genocide studies
General readers seeking to understand the Rwandan genocide
Policy makers, diplomats, and humanitarian workers
core_themes: Genocide and the mechanisms of mass violence
International apathy and failure of intervention
Aftermath and consequences for survivors and perpetrators
Complexities of Rwandan society and history
primary_purpose: To document the events of the 1994 Rwandan genocide, explore its causes and aftermath, critically examine the international community's response, and highlight the stories of survivors and the process of national reckoning with unimaginable violence.

structure_format.narrative_style: Investigative, narrative nonfiction, blending reportage, personal accounts, and historical analysis
structure_format.organization: Divided into chapters that interweave survivor testimony, journalistic observation, and reflections on justice and recovery

key_concepts_lessons: Genocide can happen rapidly and with devastating efficiency, especially when the world fails to respond.
Ordinary people can become perpetrators and victims of unimaginable atrocities.
International organizations and powerful nations can fail catastrophically in their duty to protect human rights.
After genocide, the questions of justice, reconciliation, and memory are complex and fraught.
Storytelling and journalism are critical to documenting, understanding, and learning from human tragedy.
style_tone: Detailed, empathetic, and sometimes deeply personal
notable_features: Award-winning blend of reportage and literary nonfiction
Direct testimony from survivors and witnesses
Critical examination of Western and UN failures
Exploration of the complex aftermath: justice, reconciliation, and ongoing trauma
cultural_historical_context: Written in the late 1990s, the book responded to widespread shock over the Rwandan genocide, and international outrage at the failure of the United Nations and Western nations to intervene. It contributed to the literature of bearing witness to atrocities in the wake of the Holocaust and Cold War-era conflicts. The book was published as Rwanda was actively pursuing both justice and reconciliation.
reception_impact: Recipient of the National Book Critics Circle Award for Nonfiction
Widely praised for its narrative power, depth of reporting, and compelling storytelling
Influential in shaping Western understanding of the Rwandan genocide
Frequently cited in genocide studies, journalism, human rights, and African studies curricula
Sparked ongoing debate about the responsibilities of the international community
